script.opening: (Signed, voiced by the interpreter.) “Hi. Thank you for the interpreter — that’s the first time here. I want to talk about my pill. I’ve been getting zigzag lights and then bad headaches. And I want to sort this myself — not with my mum.”

facts.text: If asked how she prefers to communicate: “BSL. English writing is my second language — long letters are hard.” Lip-reading “only a little, and not on video”. Prefers text or email from the surgery; cannot use the phone. If asked about the interpreter: happy with Aisha; she is in a private room.
“Zigzag lights, shiny, start small in the middle and spread to the side. About twenty minutes. Then they go and the headache starts.” Three times in two months; first ever about eight weeks ago.
Left or right side, throbbing, “like a heartbeat”, with nausea; wants a dark room; lasts most of the day; sleep helps. Paracetamol “doesn’t touch it”.

No weakness or numbness of an arm or hand. If asked about signing during the aura: “No, my signing is normal. My hands are fine.” Aura never more than an hour. Headache never sudden like being hit. No fever, rash, neck stiffness, head injury. No change in personality. Vision normal between attacks.
Takes it every day, 21 days then a 7-day break; no missed pills this pack. Period two weeks ago. “I can’t be pregnant — I take it properly.” Headaches not only in the pill break.
Otherwise well. BP fine at the pharmacy pill check two months ago. Non-smoker. Drinks “a bit at weekends”. Mum has migraines. No clots in the family.
Works as a teaching assistant at a school for Deaf children. Lives in a flat with a friend. New partner, Jordan, for four months — “I want proper contraception; I don’t want a baby yet.”

Only if asked about past healthcare experiences or why she wanted to come alone: “Mum always phoned and came in and signed for me. I couldn’t talk about sex or my boyfriend. Last year I was in hospital with appendicitis for three days with no interpreter. They wrote notes. I didn’t understand the operation. I was terrified.”
If options are explained clearly: interested in the implant (“my friend has one”) but wants something to start today. Does not want a coil “right now”.

Leah is bright, direct and wary. Sign at a normal pace; the interpreter voices with a short lag. If the doctor looks at or speaks to the interpreter (“Can you ask her…”), sign to the interpreter: “I’m here — talk to me.” If the doctor talks too fast or over the interpreter, look confused and sign “Sorry?”. If the doctor asks permission to involve her mother, refuse firmly. If the doctor explains clearly why the pill must stop and offers a same-day alternative, relax and engage. If the doctor asks what would make it easier to use the surgery, give clear answers: text/email, interpreter booked automatically, longer appointments, no phone calls.

ice.ideas: “Maybe the pill is giving me the headaches.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she has a new partner and wants confidential contraceptive care without her mother; after a frightening hospital stay without an interpreter she does not trust health services and needs to feel this practice will communicate with her properly. She shares the hospital story and the mother issue fully only if asked about past experiences or why she wanted to come alone.
ice.expectations: Advice about the pill and something reliable to start today; to be able to contact the surgery without her mum or the phone.

cues: “That’s the first time here” (with an interpreter) — barriers to access worth exploring.
“Not with my mum” — confidentiality, autonomy and a new relationship.
“I’m here — talk to me” (if the doctor addresses the interpreter) — direct communication matters.

checkpoints.text: Sets up the BSL consultation well: introduces everyone, checks Leah is happy with this interpreter and is private, checks the picture and lighting, speaks directly to Leah, one person at a time, and allows for the interpreting lag

Takes a clear history of typical aura (visual, spreading, about 20 minutes, followed by headache) and migraine features, and asks about red flags adapted to a BSL user (hand weakness or numbness, difficulty signing, aura over 60 minutes, thunderclap onset, fever or neck stiffness)
Checks contraceptive history and pregnancy risk (pills taken correctly, last period), BP, smoking, family history of clots, and that the headaches are not only in the pill-free interval
Explains clearly that migraine with aura makes combined hormonal contraception unsafe because of stroke risk (UKMEC 4) and advises stopping it today

Agrees a safe alternative with Leah — progestogen-only pill started immediately (with advice on extra precautions if needed), and the implant or IUS/IUD as longer-term options — and an acute migraine plan (NSAID or aspirin, triptan at headache onset, antiemetic, headache diary, avoid medication overuse)

Applies the Accessible Information Standard: records BSL as her need, flags it, books interpreters automatically, agrees text/email contact (no phone calls), longer appointments, and explains BSL routes to 111 and 999
Respects confidentiality and autonomy (no involvement of her mother), explores her past experiences, and acknowledges the hospital stay without an interpreter
Checks understanding through the interpreter (asks Leah to explain the plan back), offers written information in plain English or BSL video resources, and safety-nets with accessible routes

worked.txt: “Hello Leah, I’m Dr Lee. Hello Aisha, thank you. Leah, are you happy with Aisha interpreting today, and are you somewhere private? Can you see us both clearly? I’ll talk to you directly, and please stop me if I go too fast.”

worked.lbl: Red flags for a BSL user
worked.txt: “During the zigzags, have your hands or arms felt weak or numb? Has your signing ever been hard — finding signs or moving your hands?”

“The zigzags before your headaches are called migraine with aura. With that type of migraine, the combined pill raises the risk of a stroke. So it isn’t safe to continue — I’d like you to stop it today.”

“You can start a progesterone-only pill straight away, the day after your last combined pill. Many people later choose the implant — it lasts five years and doesn’t need remembering. Which would suit you?”
“From now on we’ll book a BSL interpreter automatically, contact you by text or email — never a phone call — and give you a double appointment. Your mum won’t be involved unless you ask.”
“Can you tell me what you’ll do with your pill tonight, and what to do if a headache comes?”

f.learning: Accessible communication is part of clinical safety. With a BSL interpreter on video: check consent and privacy, speak to the patient (not the interpreter), take turns, allow for the lag, and check understanding by teach-back. Adapt red-flag questions — for a signer, “difficulty speaking” becomes “difficulty signing” and hand weakness matters. Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception: stop it and offer a same-day progestogen-only method or LARC. Under the Accessible Information Standard the practice must identify, record, flag, share, meet and review communication needs — interpreters booked automatically, text or email contact, longer appointments — and never rely on family members to interpret.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (CoSRH, 2016, amended September 2019) · CoSRH Progestogen-only Pills guideline (2022) · NICE CG150 Headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management (2012, updated 2021) · NHS England Accessible Information Standard DAPB1605 (revised 2025) · British Sign Language Act 2022 · Equality Act 2010 · National Registers of Communication Professionals working with Deaf and Deafblind People (NRCPD)
knowledge.summary: Typical migraine with aura on the combined pill: stop it today (UKMEC 4) and start a progestogen-only method, while making the practice accessible for a Deaf BSL user.

points.t: Typical aura is fully reversible visual, sensory or speech/language symptoms developing over at least 5 minutes, each lasting 5–60 minutes, followed by headache. Visual zigzags (fortification spectra) spreading outward are classic.

Motor weakness, aura over 60 minutes, first aura after 50, aura without a typical pattern, thunderclap headache, fever and neck stiffness, new neurological signs, or headache waking from sleep with vomiting — urgent assessment. For BSL users ask about difficulty signing and hand weakness.

Migraine with aura at any age is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch, ring) because of ischaemic stroke risk. Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, injection, IUS) and copper IUD are UKMEC 1–2.

Stop the combined pill and start a progestogen-only pill (for example desogestrel 75 micrograms) the next day without a break. If the combined pill has been taken correctly in the previous 7 days no extra precautions are needed; otherwise condoms for 2 days. Offer the implant or IUS as long-acting options.

NICE CG150: aspirin 900 mg, ibuprofen or paracetamol, with a triptan (for example sumatriptan 50–100 mg) taken at the start of the headache, not during the aura; add an antiemetic if needed. Limit acute medicines to avoid medication-overuse headache; keep a diary. Consider prophylaxis if attacks are frequent.

Identify, record, flag, share, meet and review communication needs (DAPB1605, revised 2025). For BSL users: registered interpreters booked automatically, text/email or video relay contact, longer appointments, accessible written information.

Use registered interpreters (NRCPD), never family. Speak to the patient; one speaker at a time; good lighting and framing on video; avoid writing notes as a substitute for interpreting; check understanding.
Weakness, numbness, difficulty signing, aura over an hour or a sudden severe headache — 999 (999 BSL video service available). Non-urgent advice through NHS 111 BSL.

model.text: Hello Leah, I’m Dr Lee — and hello Aisha, thank you. Leah, are you happy with Aisha interpreting, and are you somewhere private? Can you see us both clearly? I’ll speak to you directly — tell me if I go too fast.
model.why: Accessible set-up: consent, privacy, picture, direct address

model.text: Yes. Thank you for the interpreter — it’s the first time here. I want to talk about my pill. I get zigzag lights then bad headaches. And I want to sort this myself, not with my mum.
Thank you for telling me — this is your appointment, and what you share stays confidential. Tell me about the zigzags.
Shiny zigzags, start in the middle and spread. About twenty minutes, then they go and the headache starts — one side, throbbing, I feel sick.
During the zigzags, have your hands or arms felt weak or numb? Has your signing ever been difficult? Have the zigzags ever lasted more than an hour, or a headache come on suddenly like a blow?
model.why: Red flags adapted for a BSL user

model.text: No. My hands are fine, my signing is normal. Never more than an hour. Never sudden.
Are you taking the pill every day without missing any, and when was your last period? Any smoking, or clots in the family?
model.why: Pregnancy risk and other UKMEC factors

model.text: Every day, no misses. Period two weeks ago. Don’t smoke. Mum has migraines. No clots.
What you describe is migraine with aura. With this type of migraine, the combined pill increases the risk of a stroke. So it isn’t safe to continue — I’d like you to stop it today. What do you think?
model.why: Clear diagnosis and the UKMEC 4 decision

model.text: Stop today? But I need contraception — I have a new partner. I don’t want a baby.

Of course. You can start a progesterone-only pill tomorrow with no gap — because you’ve taken your pill properly, you’ll stay protected. Longer term, the implant or the hormone coil are very reliable. What would suit you?
model.why: Same-day safe alternative and LARC options

model.text: Start the new pill now. Maybe the implant later — my friend has one.

For the headaches: take ibuprofen or aspirin with an anti-sickness tablet early, and I’ll prescribe sumatriptan to take when the headache starts — not during the zigzags. Keep a diary. Can I ask — what has it been like getting healthcare in the past?
model.why: Acute plan, then explores past experiences

model.text: Mum always phoned and signed for me — I couldn’t talk about sex. Last year in hospital three days with no interpreter. They wrote notes. I was terrified.

I’m really sorry — that should never happen. Here, we’ll record that you need a BSL interpreter and book one every time, contact you by text or email only, give you double appointments, and your mum won’t be involved unless you want her. You can also use NHS 111 and 999 through BSL video services.
Can you tell me what you’ll do with your pills tonight, and what you’ll do if a headache comes?
Stop the old pill. Start the new one tomorrow, every day, same time. Headache — ibuprofen and the new tablet when the pain starts.

Exactly. If you ever get weakness, numbness, trouble signing, zigzags over an hour or a sudden severe headache — call 999 using the BSL service. I’ll message you to book an implant appointment with an interpreter, and review the headaches in six weeks.

social.t: Many Deaf people see themselves as a linguistic and cultural minority rather than disabled. BSL is a full language, not signed English; written English may be a second language.
Relying on relatives removes privacy, especially for sexual health, mental health and safeguarding, and risks errors.

legal.t: Recognises BSL as a language of England, Wales and Scotland.
Duty to make reasonable adjustments, including interpreters, without charging the patient.
A competent adult’s health information is not shared with her parent without consent.

professional.t: Mandatory for NHS and publicly funded adult social care: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review communication needs (DAPB1605, revised 2025).
Use NRCPD-registered BSL interpreters; record the interpreter’s name; brief them; allow extra time.

community.t: SignHealth (BSL health information), RNID, NHS 111 BSL service, 999 BSL video relay, The Migraine Trust, Brook and local sexual health services.

playbook.diagnosis: Migraine with typical visual aura in a woman using combined oral contraception — UKMEC 4: the combined pill must stop.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “These are migraines with aura. With this type, the combined pill increases stroke risk, so we’ll switch to a safer method today.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted to sort this yourself, without your mum — and you can.”

Acute migraine plan: NSAID/aspirin, sumatriptan at headache onset, antiemetic; diary

safetyNet: Weakness, numbness, trouble signing, aura over an hour or thunderclap headache — 999 via BSL service

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed when the communication is about the interpreter rather than the patient, or when the doctor continues the combined pill.

items.fail: Talking to the interpreter: “Can you ask her if…”
items.why: Excludes the patient; she notices and disengages.
items.fix: Look at and speak to Leah.

items.why: Misses signing difficulty and hand weakness — the BSL equivalents.
items.fix: Ask about signing and hand function during aura.

items.fail: Continuing the combined pill, or switching to another combined method.
items.why: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for all combined hormonal contraception.
items.fix: Stop today; start a progestogen-only method.

items.fail: Stopping the pill with no same-day alternative.
items.why: Leaves her at risk of pregnancy.
Without AIS actions she will be back to phone calls and her mother.
items.fix: Record, flag, book interpreters, text/email contact.

items.fail: Suggesting her mother could help next time.
items.why: Breaches her stated wishes and confidentiality.
items.fix: Confirm her mother is not involved unless she asks.

wordPics.clearFail: Talks to the interpreter, continues the combined pill, or stops it with no alternative; no red-flag screen; ignores confidentiality.
wordPics.fail: Recognises migraine with aura but gives an unclear contraceptive plan, misses BSL-adapted red flags or the access problem.
wordPics.pass: Sets up the interpreted video well, diagnoses migraine with aura, stops the combined pill and starts a progestogen-only method, gives a migraine plan and safety-net.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: adapts red flags to signing, explores her past experiences and wish for privacy, implements the Accessible Information Standard concretely, uses teach-back, and offers LARC with an interpreter booked.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: adapts red flags to signing, explores her past experiences and wish for privacy, implements the Accessible Information Standard concretely, uses teach-back, and offers LARC with an interpreter booked.
